newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition keeps up election protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition keeps up election protests.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties launched fresh protests on Friday to demand President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists accept defeat in municipal elections.
Some 1,000 university students marched through the centre of Belgrade to back the opposition coalition which accuses the Socialists of trying to annul their victory in local polls.
Student leaders joined an opposition demonstration to protest the "violation of basic democratic principles and unscrupulous trampling of elementary human rights".
Friday's protests marked the fifth day of demonstrations in Belgrade and towns across Serbia since the opposition claimed victory in run-off local elections held on Sunday.
The opposition said electoral commissions and courts might deliver rulings on ballot results as soon as Friday.

Leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition say the authorities have committed massive fraud with the goal of annulling votes which gave the opposition victories in 15 of the 18 biggest towns in Serbia.
The Socialists conceded defeat in Belgrade and the northern town of Novi Sad, but elsewhere electoral commissions had yet to announce final results.
In the industrial town of Nis, where the opposition said it won, a local electoral commission gave the Socialists victory by awarding them extra seats due to unspecified irregularities.
Some 20,000 people marched through Belgrade on Thursday, in the city's biggest demonstration in years.
Zoran Djindjic, one of three opposition coalition leaders and expected to become the new mayor of Belgrade, said protests would continue until the Socialists verified the poll results.
Students last took to the streets in the wake of 1991 demonstrations which Milosevic crushed with massive police force and tanks. Two men were killed.
The students then staged a round-the-clock sit-in in the centre of Belgrade, forcing him to make concessions.

"The tenacity and endurance of the demonstrations is sorely testing the authorities. The most alarming fact for them is that the numbers of demonstrators in Belgrade is growing instead of diminishing," one diplomat said.

Milosevic has already been warned by the United States to improve his poor human rights record if he wants to see the lifting of an "outer wall" of sanctions which bars Belgrade from desperately-needed foreign capital.
The United States and Britain have voiced grave concerns over the opposition's allegations.
Britain's ambassador wrote to the Zajedno leaders saying he was concerned by "the uncertainty and allegations over the results of the Serbian municipal elections".
Ivor Roberts said he had initiated an urgent discussion with the European Union, which was expected to issue a joint statement in Brussels.
Some tensions were likely to be defused by the reported return of the wife of opposition leader Vuk Draskovic.
Draskovic, who leads the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO) in the Zajedno coalition, on Thursday accused the authorities of "kidnapping" his wife Danica -- a political figure in her own right.

On Friday an SPO official confirmed Danica had telephoned from her home to say she had been released and was safe and well. There was no independent confirmation of the alleged kidnapping and subsequent release.
